lessons.title: Water quality for farm uses
lessons.html:
Not all water is fit for every use

Water quality affects crop yields, soil health, animal production, irrigation equipment and human health. Water that is fine for cattle may be unsuitable for drip irrigation or for workers to drink. South African farm water comes from boreholes, rivers, dams, canals and rainwater tanks, each with typical problems.

Key quality parameters

ParameterWhy it matters
Salinity (electrical conductivity, EC)Salt damage to crops, soil salinisation, lower animal intake
Sodium (SAR)Breaks down soil structure, reduces infiltration
pHAffects chemical effectiveness, nutrient availability, corrosion
Hardness, iron, manganeseScale and blockages in drippers and pipes
NitrateCan be toxic to livestock and infants; sign of contamination
Microbes (E. coli, coliforms)Disease risk to people, animals and fresh produce
Suspended solids, algaeBlocked filters, toxic blue-green algae blooms in dams

Guidelines

The Department of Water and Sanitation has published South African water quality guidelines for agricultural uses (irrigation, livestock watering, aquaculture) and SANS 241 sets drinking water standards. Compare laboratory results with the guideline for the specific use. Fresh produce for export or retail often has extra requirements for irrigation water microbial quality.

Testing

Take samples in clean bottles supplied by an accredited laboratory, following their instructions, especially for microbial tests that must be kept cool and delivered quickly. Test each source at least once a year and more often if there is a problem or after floods. Record results so trends can be tracked.

lessons.title: Sources of contamination and prevention
lessons.html:
Protecting water at the source

Preventing contamination is cheaper and more reliable than treatment.

Main sources on farms

  • Animal waste: kraals, feedlots, dairy effluent and piggeries near boreholes or streams.
  • Human sewage: poorly sited pit latrines or septic tanks.
  • Fertilisers: nitrate and phosphate runoff causing algae blooms.
  • Agrochemicals: mixing and rinsing sprayers near water, spills, drift.
  • Fuel and oil from workshops and diesel tanks.
  • Erosion: silt reduces dam capacity and carries pollutants.
  • Upstream users such as mines, towns or other farms.

Prevention measures

  • Site kraals, dairies, septic tanks and chemical stores well away from boreholes and downslope of them.
  • Seal borehole heads and fence a protection zone around them.
  • Keep riparian buffers of natural vegetation along rivers and dams.
  • Contain effluent in lined dams; irrigate it onto land at rates the soil can take.
  • Mix chemicals on a bunded pad away from water; never wash equipment in streams.
  • Apply fertiliser according to soil analysis, not routine.
  • Bund fuel tanks and have spill kits.

Legal duties

The National Water Act 36 of 1998 makes it an offence to pollute water resources and places a duty of care on landowners and users to prevent pollution. Certain activities, such as disposing of waste water, may need authorisation. Report significant pollution incidents to the Department of Water and Sanitation.

lessons.title: Treating and managing water quality
lessons.html:
Improving water for its use

Irrigation water

  • Filtration: sand, disc or screen filters remove particles before drip systems; backflush regularly.
  • Acid injection can lower pH and prevent scale in hard water; must be done by trained staff with PPE.
  • Chlorination controls bacteria and slime in pipes, and can improve microbial quality of irrigation water for fresh produce.
  • Salinity management: irrigate with a leaching fraction to move salts below the root zone, ensure good drainage, choose salt-tolerant crops and, where sodium is high, apply gypsum as advised by an agronomist.

Livestock water

Clean troughs regularly, keep dung and dead birds out, shade troughs to reduce algae, and check that flow is enough for hot days. Test water if animals drink less than normal or production drops. Where salinity or nitrate is high, consider alternative sources or blending.

Drinking water for people

Supply workers with water that meets SANS 241. Treat with filtration and disinfection (chlorination or UV) where needed, keep storage tanks covered and clean, and test regularly.

Dams and algae

Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) blooms can produce toxins that kill livestock and dogs. Reduce nutrient inflow, keep animals away from scummy water and provide alternative water during blooms.

Safety with treatment chemicals

Store chlorine and acids separately, never mix them (toxic gas can form), always add acid to water and not water to acid, and wear gloves and eye protection.

Monitoring plan

Draw up a schedule listing each source, its uses, parameters to test, frequency and action levels. Review results annually.

Key points

  • Match water quality to each use using SA guidelines and SANS 241 for drinking water.
  • Test sources regularly through an accredited laboratory.
  • Prevent contamination by siting, buffers and good chemical handling.
  • Filter, chlorinate and leach salts as needed for irrigation.
  • Never mix chlorine and acid; keep stock away from algae blooms.
